summary: Presents INETPhone, a proposed telephone service for voice communication across the Internet, including telephone servers and the services around them. It is an informational description of the design and does not define an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: Instead of using the phone company's wires, you talk to a friend through the Internet. This memo describes one early way to make phone calls that way.

questions: how did early internet telephony work
how do phone networks connect to the internet
how does voip map area codes
subtitle: A telephone service that uses the Internet to connect callers while keeping local phone networks for access.

tldr.problem: Voice communication over the Internet in the mid-1990s required computers with Internet connections. Most people used ordinary phones, and existing phone services were expensive for long distance.
tldr.mechanism: INETPhone places servers in telephone area codes that act as gateways. Callers make a local phone call to their nearest INETPhone server, which then connects via the Internet to another server in the destination area code, which places a local call to the recipient.
tldr.outcome: The proposal was informational only and did not become a standard. Later technologies like H.323 and SIP became the dominant protocols for Internet telephony. The concept of VoIP gateways using this model influenced commercial systems.

facts.label: Network architecture
facts.value: Local phone call + Internet connection + local phone call

today: RFC 1789 is Informational and has not been updated or obsoleted. While INETPhone as proposed was never deployed, its vision of integrating telephone services with the Internet became reality through later protocols like H.323 and SIP, and commercial VoIP services including gateways between traditional telephony and Internet-based systems.

sections.title: Introduction and Overview
sections.content:
INETPhone is a telephone service proposed in 1995 to bring voice communication through the Internet to ordinary telephone users. The key innovation is that it integrates existing local telephone networks with the Internet, avoiding the need for users to own computers or special equipment.

The service is motivated by two goals: to demonstrate that voice communication on the Internet can be a major step toward integrated multimedia services on the Internet, and to provide the Internet community with cheap and convenient voice communication, avoiding long-distance telephone charges.

The RFC describes a specific scenario: a user in area A picks up a phone and calls a local number (the INETPhone server in their area). After connecting, they enter a phone number in area B. The server in area A then connects to the INETPhone server in area B over the Internet and requests it to dial the destination number as a local call. This converts a long-distance call into two local calls and one Internet connection.
sections.eli5: You call a local computer instead of long distance. It connects through the Internet to a computer near your friend, which calls your friend locally.

sections.title: Design Philosophy
sections.content:
INETPhone differs from other Internet voice systems of the 1990s in three ways. First, it integrates existing telephone networks with the Internet, providing access through ordinary phones and conventional telephone service, making it accessible to far more users than computer-based voice systems.

Second, it uses a client-server architecture. INETPhone servers, located in telephone area codes, act as gateways between the telephone network and the Internet. Servers accept incoming calls, identify users, collect destination phone numbers, route calls to remote servers, maintain voice packet exchanges with the Internet, interact with directory servers, handle exceptions like long delays or dropped packets, monitor quality of service, and keep accounting information.

Third, it proposes an open-partnership scheme to avoid monopolization by large companies. Any organization or individual can install an INETPhone server and join the partnership. All members have equal rights to use the service at the same rates (based on bytes transmitted), and a not-for-profit consortium of member representatives would establish regulations and specifications for the service.
sections.eli5: Use regular phones so anyone can participate, use servers that connect phones to the Internet, and let everyone share in running the system fairly.

sections.title: INETPhone Servers and Directory Servers
sections.content:
An INETPhone server requires hardware interfaces to both the telephone network and the Internet. Commercial telephone interface cards (such as Dialogic Voice Boards) provide the necessary functionality: detecting and generating telephone signals (ring, DTMF tones), receiving and initiating phone calls, recording or playing back audio signals, and monitoring call progress.

The server's functions include receiving local calls, identifying the caller's PIN (personal identification number) to determine whether to proceed, accepting a destination phone number, looking up the appropriate remote server in the directory, establishing a connection to that remote server, making a local call at the remote site, and maintaining full-duplex, real-time voice packet exchange over the Internet. Additional features noted for future consideration include compression/decompression of voice, security, multicasting to multiple recipients, and voice mail.

Directory Servers maintain a mapping between IP addresses and telephone area codes of INETPhone servers. When a server is installed, it registers itself with a Directory Server. The Directory Servers disseminate this mapping information to INETPhone servers so they can look up which remote server to contact for a given phone number. Servers may cache this information locally to reduce queries.
sections.eli5: Each server has a phone card to handle calls and an Internet connection. Directory servers work like a phonebook, mapping area codes to server computer addresses.

sections.title: Open Partnership Model
sections.content:
The RFC proposes that INETPhone be built on a voluntary, open-partnership scheme rather than controlled by a small number of large companies. Key principles include:

Voluntary participation: Any organization or individual can join or leave the partnership at any time. To join, they must install and maintain an INETPhone server on the Internet with equal capacity for inbound and outbound calls.

Equal rights: Each member has the same right to use INETPhone services through any server on the Internet. All services are priced identically, based on the number of bytes transmitted and whatever rates the Internet authority (such as ISPs) charge.

Consortium governance: A not-for-profit consortium formed from member representatives establishes regulations, specifications, and standards for INETPhone service and coordinates enforcement of these rules by all members.

The RFC notes that hundreds or thousands of INETPhone servers would be required for nationwide coverage (roughly one per telephone area code in the United States), making this distributed, participatory model more practical than having a single organization deploy all servers.
sections.eli5: Anyone can set up a server and join. Everyone gets equal service for the same price. A group of members make the rules together.
